options.text: `const c: Counter = { interval: 1, reset() {} };`
options.why: An object literal has no call signature, so it is missing `(start: number): string`.

options.text: Declare `const c = (s: number) => String(s)`, then assign `c.interval` and `c.reset`
options.why: TypeScript tracks property assignments on a `const` function, so `c` gains both members and is assignable to `Counter`.

options.text: `class C implements Counter { interval = 1; reset() {} }`
options.why: Class instances cannot carry a call signature, so the class does not satisfy `Counter`.

options.text: `const c: Counter = function (s: number) { return String(s); };` with nothing else added
options.why: The function expression has the call signature but lacks `interval` and `reset`.

explanation: A hybrid type combines a call signature with properties, which is how libraries like jQuery or Express apps are typed. Since TypeScript 3.1, property assignments made right after a `function` declaration or a `const` arrow function are added to that function's type ("expando" properties). After `c.interval = 1; c.reset = () => {};` the value has type `{ (start: number): string; interval: number; reset: () => void }`, which is assignable to `Counter` with no `as` cast.
reference: TS Handbook: Hybrid Types; TS 3.1 release notes (properties on functions)

options.text: Nothing: a function is always assignable to an interface that has a call signature
options.why: Structural checks also compare every required property, not only the call signature.

options.text: TS2322 on `c3.interval = 1`, because functions cannot have properties
options.why: Assigning properties to a `const` function is allowed and is added to its type.

options.text: TS2741: property `reset` is missing in the type of `c3` but required in `Counter`
options.why: `c3` has the call signature and `interval`, but no `reset`, so it is not assignable to `Counter`.

options.text: TS2349: `Counter` is not callable because it also declares properties
options.why: Interfaces can declare a call signature next to properties; that is exactly what a hybrid type is.

explanation: TypeScript infers `c3` as `{ (start: number): string; interval: number }` from the arrow function plus the expando assignment. Assigning it to `Counter` checks the call signature and each required property. `reset` is missing, so tsc reports TS2741: "Property 'reset' is missing in type … but required in type 'Counter'". Add `c3.reset = () => {}` before the assignment to fix it.

stem: A TypeScript interface can describe a value that can be called like a function and also has properties, such as `interface Logger { (msg: string): void; level: string }`.

options.text: True
options.why: An interface can mix a call signature with ordinary properties; this is called a hybrid type.

options.text: False
options.why: Interfaces are not limited to object shapes: call and construct signatures can sit alongside properties.

explanation: Functions in JavaScript are objects, so they can carry properties. TypeScript models this with an interface (or type literal) that has a call signature plus properties. Values like `express()` apps or a `debounce` result with a `.cancel()` method are typed this way.

options.text: `new Point(1, 2)`
options.why: Matches the first overload, `(x: number, y: number)`.

options.text: `new Point([1, 2])`
options.why: Matches the second overload, `(coords: [number, number])`.

options.text: `new Point(1)`
options.why: Only the implementation accepts a single number, and it is not callable from outside.

options.text: `new Point([1, 2], 3)`
options.why: No overload takes a tuple followed by a number.

options.text: `new Point("1", "2")`
options.why: Neither overload accepts strings.

explanation: With overloads, only the overload signatures are visible to callers. The implementation signature `(a: number | [number, number], b?: number)` is hidden. So `new Point(1)` fails with TS2345, and tsc adds a note: "The call would have succeeded against this implementation, but implementation signatures of overloads are not externally visible."

options.text: A class may declare at most one constructor signature
options.why: Classes can overload constructors just like functions.

options.text: The implementation's first parameter is `number`, so it can't accept the overload's tuple
options.why: Every overload must be assignable to the implementation signature.

options.text: Overload signatures must be listed after the implementation
options.why: It is the reverse: overloads come first and the implementation is last.

options.text: Overloaded constructors cannot declare optional parameters such as `b?: number` in the implementation
options.why: Optional parameters are fine; the conflict is the parameter type.

explanation: The implementation must be general enough to handle every overload. Here an overload accepts `[number, number]` as its first argument, but the implementation's first parameter is `number`, so that overload is incompatible and tsc reports TS2394. Widen the implementation to `a: number | [number, number]` and branch on `Array.isArray(a)`.

options.text: `[x: number, y: number]`, the first overload
options.why: Inference from an overloaded signature uses the last overload, not the first.

options.text: `[coords: [number, number]]`, the last overload
options.why: Conditional types infer from the last signature of an overloaded type.

options.text: A union of both overloads' parameter tuples
options.why: TypeScript does not combine overloads when inferring with `infer`.

options.text: `[a: number | [number, number], b?: number]`, the implementation
options.why: The implementation signature is not part of the class's visible type.

explanation: `ConstructorParameters` is a conditional type that uses `infer` on the construct signature. When a type has several overloads, inference picks the last one (the most general by convention), so `P` is `[coords: [number, number]]`. The same applies to `Parameters` and `ReturnType` on overloaded functions. List the overload you want inferred last, or extract the parameter types yourself.
reference: TS Handbook: Conditional Types (inferring within conditional types)

options.text: Turning on `noImplicitReturns` in tsconfig so every async call must be returned
options.why: That option checks code paths that miss a `return`, not promises.

options.text: typescript-eslint's `no-floating-promises` rule with typed linting
options.why: The rule uses type information to see that the call returns a promise that is never handled.

options.text: Turning on `noUnusedLocals` in tsconfig
options.why: An unused expression result is not an unused local variable.

options.text: Prettier, which inserts a missing `await`
options.why: Prettier only formats code; it never changes behaviour.

explanation: Calling an async function without `await`, `.catch()` or `void` is legal TypeScript, so the compiler stays silent, even under `strict`. typescript-eslint's `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` rule catches it, but it needs type information. Typed linting means configuring the parser with `projectService` (or `project`) so rules can query the TypeScript program.
reference: typescript-eslint docs: no-floating-promises; Linting with Type Information

stem: Which two typescript-eslint rules need typed linting (type information from the TypeScript program) to work? (Choose two.)

options.text: `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises`
options.why: It has to know an expression's type is a promise.

options.text: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment`
options.why: It detects values typed `any` flowing into typed variables, which requires types.

options.text: `@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any`
options.why: It only looks for the literal `any` keyword in the syntax tree.

options.text: `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports`
options.why: It works from import syntax and identifier usage, without the type checker.

options.text: `@typescript-eslint/ban-ts-comment`
options.why: It matches comment text such as `@ts-ignore`; no types are needed.

explanation: typescript-eslint rules fall into two groups. Syntax-only rules look at the AST and run fast. Type-aware rules, such as `no-floating-promises`, `no-misused-promises` and the `no-unsafe-*` family, ask the TypeScript type checker about expressions, so they need typed linting configured and are slower because a full program is built.
reference: typescript-eslint docs: Linting with Type Information

stem: A team already runs typescript-eslint with typed linting in CI, so they delete the separate `tsc --noEmit` step to save time. What do they lose?

options.text: Nothing, because typed linting reports every type error tsc would
options.why: Lint rules use type information but do not report the compiler's own diagnostics.

options.text: Type errors such as wrong argument types now pass CI unnoticed
options.why: ESLint only reports its rules; the compiler's type errors are never surfaced.

options.text: Formatting checks, because tsc enforced the code style
options.why: tsc has never checked formatting.

options.text: Only the emitted `.js` files, which CI did not use anyway
options.why: `--noEmit` already produced no files, so that is not what changes.

explanation: typed linting builds a TypeScript program so rules can ask about types, but ESLint only reports problems its rules look for. A call such as `add("1", 2)` that tsc rejects with TS2345 passes ESLint silently. Keep `tsc --noEmit` (or `tsc -b`) as its own CI step alongside linting.
reference: typescript-eslint docs: Linting with Type Information

stem: Running Prettier on a `.ts` file also reports type errors in that file.

options.text: True
options.why: Prettier parses TypeScript only to reprint it; it never runs the type checker.

options.text: False
options.why: Prettier formats code. Type errors come from tsc (or an editor using it).

explanation: Prettier is a formatter: it parses TypeScript syntax and reprints it consistently, but it does no type checking. Projects usually run Prettier for formatting, ESLint (with `eslint-config-prettier` to turn off conflicting style rules) for code quality, and `tsc --noEmit` for types.

stem: `script.ts` contains a type error but would run fine as JavaScript. What happens with `npx ts-node script.ts` (default settings) compared with `npx tsx script.ts`?

options.text: Both run it, because neither tool type-checks
options.why: ts-node type-checks by default unless you opt out.

options.text: Both refuse to run it, because both invoke the TypeScript compiler before executing
options.why: tsx transpiles with esbuild and never type-checks.

options.text: ts-node stops with a `TSError`; tsx runs it, since it only strips types
options.why: ts-node type-checks by default; tsx transpiles with esbuild without checking.

options.text: ts-node runs it with a warning; tsx stops with a type error
options.why: The behaviours are the other way round.

explanation: ts-node compiles through the TypeScript language service, so by default it reports type errors (as `TSError`) and refuses to run. Its `--transpileOnly` option skips checking. tsx transpiles with esbuild, which removes types without checking them, so type errors never stop it. Either way, run `tsc --noEmit` in CI to catch type errors.
reference: ts-node docs (type checking, transpileOnly); tsx docs

stem: A dev server started with `ts-node src/server.ts` takes 20 seconds to boot in a large project. Which change makes it fast without losing type safety?

options.text: Keep ts-node but set `"skipLibCheck": false` and `"incremental": true` so its type-check results are cached between boots
options.why: `skipLibCheck: false` makes checking slower, not faster.

options.text: Switch the project to `"module": "commonjs"`
options.why: The module format barely affects how long type-checking takes.

options.text: Use a transpile-only runner (tsx or `ts-node --transpileOnly`) and keep `tsc --noEmit` in CI
options.why: Boot skips the type checker, while a separate tsc run still enforces types.

options.text: Add `// @ts-nocheck` to every file so ts-node skips it
options.why: That silences type errors everywhere, losing all type safety.

explanation: Most of ts-node's start-up time is spent type-checking the whole program. Running the server through a transpile-only path (tsx, ts-node `--transpileOnly`, or Node's built-in type stripping) removes that cost. Type safety then comes from a separate `tsc --noEmit` (in watch mode locally, and in CI), so checking and running are decoupled.

stem: Match each command with what it does to a `.ts` file.

options.text: Type-checks and reports errors, emitting no JavaScript
Transpiles with esbuild and runs it, never type-checking
Type-checks by default, then runs it
Removes erasable type syntax and runs it, rejecting enums and namespaces

explanation: There are three common ways to run TypeScript, and only some type-check. `tsc --noEmit` only checks. ts-node type-checks by default (unless `--transpileOnly`). tsx uses esbuild and never checks. Recent Node.js versions run `.ts` files directly by stripping erasable type syntax; constructs that need code generation, such as `enum`, `namespace` and parameter properties, are rejected unless you opt into transformation.
reference: Node.js docs: Modules – TypeScript; ts-node docs; tsx docs

stem: Which command generates a starter `tsconfig.json` in the current folder? Type the full command, starting with `tsc`.
explanation: `tsc --init` writes a commented `tsconfig.json` with recommended defaults. Run it through the project's own copy of TypeScript (`npx tsc --init`) so the generated options match the installed version.

stem: A developer has TypeScript 5.4 installed globally, while the project lists `"typescript": "6.0.3"` in `devDependencies`. CI fails on errors their local `tsc` never showed. What is the fix?

options.text: Upgrade the global install, since tsc always prefers the global version
options.why: Relying on a global install keeps local and CI versions drifting apart.

options.text: Run the pinned copy via `npx tsc` and set the editor to the workspace TypeScript
options.why: Both then use the pinned 6.0.3 compiler that CI uses.

options.text: Delete `typescript` from `devDependencies` so that CI falls back to the same global version everyone uses
options.why: CI machines may not have any global TypeScript, and versions would still be unpinned.

options.text: Add `"skipLibCheck": true` so the versions behave the same
options.why: That only skips checking `.d.ts` files; it does not align compiler versions.

explanation: Each TypeScript version adds checks and changes defaults, so the compiler version is part of the build. Install TypeScript as a pinned `devDependency`, run it via `npx tsc` or `npm run typecheck` (which resolve `node_modules/.bin`), and set the editor to use the workspace TypeScript version.

options.text: Both compile, and the conflicting members merge so `C['id']` and `D['id']` are `string | number`
options.why: Neither form unions conflicting property types.

options.text: `interface C` errors with TS2320; `D` compiles and `D['id']` is `never`
options.why: Interfaces reject conflicting inherited members; intersections intersect them.

options.text: Both are errors, because `id` has two different types
options.why: Intersections never report this conflict; they quietly produce `never`.

options.text: Both compile, and the later interface wins, so `id` is `number`
options.why: Interface `extends` does not override in order; it requires identical members.

explanation: When an interface extends several interfaces, members with the same name must be identical, otherwise tsc reports TS2320: "Interface 'C' cannot simultaneously extend types 'A' and 'B'". An intersection type never reports this: it intersects the property types, so `id` becomes `string & number`, which is `never`, and the mistake only shows up later. This early error is one reason to prefer `extends` for composing object types.
reference: TS Handbook: Extending Types; Intersection Types

stem: Given `type User = { id: string; name: string }` and `interface Base { kind: string }`, which two declarations compile? (Choose two.)

options.text: `interface Sub extends Base { kind: "sub" }`
options.why: A subtype may narrow an inherited property to a compatible literal type.

options.text: `interface X extends Pick<User, "id"> { extra: number }`
options.why: `Pick<User, "id">` is an object type with statically known members, so it can be extended.

options.text: `interface Bad extends Base { kind: number }`
options.why: `number` is not assignable to `string`, so tsc reports TS2430.

options.text: `interface U2 extends ({ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }) {}`
options.why: An interface cannot extend a union type (TS2312).

options.text: `interface Y extends Record<string, number> { name: string }`
options.why: `name: string` conflicts with the inherited `number` index signature (TS2411).

explanation: An interface can extend any object type whose members are statically known, including mapped types like `Pick<…>`. Members it redeclares must stay assignable to the inherited ones: narrowing `kind: string` to `"sub"` is fine, but changing it to `number` is TS2430. Unions cannot be extended (TS2312), and a property that conflicts with an inherited index signature is TS2411.
reference: TS Handbook: Extending Types; Object Types

stem: Which declaration makes `Admin` include every member of both `User` and `Permissions`?

options.text: `interface Admin extends User, Permissions {}`
options.why: An interface can extend several types at once, separated by commas.

options.text: `interface Admin implements User, Permissions {}`
options.why: `implements` is for classes; interfaces use `extends`.

options.text: `interface Admin extends User extends Permissions {}`
options.why: `extends` appears once, followed by a comma-separated list.

options.text: `interface Admin = User + Permissions`
options.why: There is no `+` operator for types; use `extends` or `&`.

explanation: Interfaces support multiple inheritance with `extends A, B, C`. The new interface gets every member of each base type and can add or narrow members of its own. `type Admin = User & Permissions` is the type-alias equivalent.

options.text: `{ kind: "circle"; r: number }`
options.why: `Extract` keeps the union members assignable to `{ kind: "circle" }`.

options.text: `{ kind: "circle" }`
options.why: `Extract` returns the matching members themselves, not the filter type.

options.text: `{ kind: "square"; s: number }`
options.why: That is what `Exclude` would keep.

options.text: `never`, since neither member equals `{ kind: "circle" }` exactly
options.why: The test is assignability, not exact equality.

explanation: `Extract<T, U>` is `T extends U ? T : never`, distributed over each member of the union `T`. The circle member is assignable to `{ kind: "circle" }`, so it is kept whole; the square member is not. This is the standard way to pull one variant out of a discriminated union.

stem:
What does `F` resolve to?

```ts
type F = Extract<string | number | (() => void), Function>;
```

options.text: `string | number`
options.why: Those are the members that are not functions, which is what `Exclude` would return.

options.text: `Function`
options.why: `Extract` keeps the original union member, not the filter type.

options.text: `() => void`
options.why: Only the function type is assignable to the global `Function` interface.

options.text: `never`, because `Function` is an interface and not a union
options.why: `U` does not need to be a union; `T` is the union being distributed.

explanation: `Extract` distributes over `T`: `string extends Function` is false, `number extends Function` is false, and `() => void extends Function` is true. The result is `() => void`. Its counterpart `Exclude<T, Function>` gives `string | number`.

stem: Given `class Dog { bark() { return "woof"; } }`, what is the difference between `typeof Dog` and `InstanceType<typeof Dog>`?

options.text: They are the same type, because a class name always refers to its instances in every position
options.why: In type position `Dog` means the instance type; `typeof Dog` means the constructor.

options.text: `typeof Dog` is the constructor; `InstanceType<typeof Dog>` is `Dog` itself
options.why: InstanceType extracts what `new` on that constructor returns.

options.text: `typeof Dog` is the string `"function"`; `InstanceType` is the class
options.why: `typeof` in a type position gives the static type, not a runtime string.

options.text: `InstanceType<typeof Dog>` lists the constructor's parameters
options.why: That is `ConstructorParameters`.

explanation: A class declares two things: a value (the constructor function) and a type (its instances). In type positions, `Dog` is the instance type and `typeof Dog` is the constructor's type, including static members. `InstanceType<C>` takes a construct-signature type and returns what `new` produces, which is useful in generic factories that receive a class.

options.text: `InstanceType` does not accept abstract classes
options.why: `InstanceType<typeof Animal>` is valid and gives `Animal`.

options.text: An abstract constructor type cannot be assigned to `new () => any`
options.why: TS2345: "Cannot assign an abstract constructor type to a non-abstract constructor type."

options.text: `Animal` has no zero-argument constructor
options.why: Its implicit constructor takes no arguments; abstractness is the problem.

options.text: Generic constraints cannot mention constructor types such as `new () => any`
options.why: Constructor types are common constraints in factories and mixins.

explanation: `typeof Animal` has an abstract construct signature, because you cannot `new` an abstract class. `new () => any` promises the function can call `new k()`, so the abstract class is rejected with TS2345. `Dog` is concrete and passes. If a function only needs to inspect a class and never instantiate it, constrain with `abstract new (...args: any) => any` instead.

options.text: `...`, because `a` is declared as `Animal`
options.why: The declared type affects checking only; the runtime object is a `Cat`.

options.text: `meow`
options.why: Method calls dispatch on the runtime object, so the override runs.

options.text: A compile error: a `Cat` cannot be stored in an `Animal` variable
options.why: A subclass instance is assignable to its base class type.

options.text: `... meow`, because both methods run
options.why: An override replaces the base method unless it calls `super.speak()`.

explanation: This is polymorphism: code written against the base type works with any subclass, and each object answers with its own implementation. Annotating `a` as `Animal` only limits which members you may access at compile time. JavaScript looks up `speak` on the actual object's prototype chain at runtime, finding `Cat.prototype.speak`.

stem: Given `class P1 { f(x: string) { return x; } }`, which three subclasses compile under `strict`? (Choose three.)

options.text: `class P3 extends P1 { f(x: "a") { return x; } }`
options.why: Method parameters are checked bivariantly, so a narrower parameter is allowed.

options.text: `class P4 extends P1 { f(x: string | number) { return String(x); } }`
options.why: A wider parameter is always a safe override.

options.text: `class P5 extends P1 { f() { return "none"; } }`
options.why: An override may take fewer parameters; extra arguments are ignored.

options.text: `class P6 extends P1 { f(x: string, y: string) { return x + y; } }`
options.why: A second required parameter would break callers that pass one argument (TS2416).

options.text: `class P7 extends P1 { f(x: string) { return 1; } }`
options.why: The return type `number` is not assignable to `string` (TS2416).

explanation: An override must be assignable to the base member. Returning a different type and requiring more parameters both fail with TS2416. Taking fewer or wider parameters is safe. A narrower parameter (`"a"`) is unsound but still accepted, because methods are compared bivariantly even under `strictFunctionTypes`. Only function-typed properties get the strict check.
reference: TS Handbook: Type Compatibility (method parameter bivariance)

options.text: `super` cannot be used inside arrow functions
options.why: `super` works in arrows inside class bodies; `super.method()` would be fine there.

options.text: `handle` is an instance field, not a method on `H1.prototype`
options.why: `super.x` reads from the parent prototype, where a class field never lives.

options.text: Arrow-function fields cannot be overridden in subclasses, so redeclaring `handle` in `H2` is the error
options.why: Redeclaring the field is allowed; reaching the parent version via `super` is not.

options.text: The field initializers run in the wrong order
options.why: Initialisation order is not what TS2855 reports.

explanation: Methods such as `method()` live on `H1.prototype`, so `super.method()` finds them. Class fields such as `handle = () => …` are created on each instance by the constructor and never exist on the prototype, so `super.handle` would be `undefined` at runtime. TypeScript catches this with TS2855: "Class field 'handle' defined by the parent class is not accessible in the child class via super." Make `handle` a method if subclasses need to extend it.
reference: TS Handbook: Classes (fields vs methods); MDN: super

stem: A team adds `@total-typescript/ts-reset` and imports it once in a global `.d.ts` file. What changes?

options.text: It validates JSON payloads at runtime against the TypeScript types declared for them
options.why: ts-reset is types only; it adds no runtime checks.

options.text: Built-in typings get stricter, e.g. `JSON.parse` returns `unknown`
options.why: It overrides parts of the standard library declarations across the project.

options.text: It resets every compiler option to TypeScript's defaults
options.why: It doesn't touch tsconfig at all.

options.text: It removes all `any` types from third-party packages
options.why: It only adjusts a handful of standard library signatures.

explanation: ts-reset is a set of declaration overrides for the standard library. It makes `JSON.parse` and `fetch().json()` return `unknown` instead of `any`, lets `.filter(Boolean)` remove falsy members, and widens `includes` on readonly arrays. Because it changes global types, it suits applications, not libraries that others consume.

stem: Match each package with its main purpose.

options.text: Runtime schema validation that also infers static types
A library of extra utility types such as `SetRequired` and `PartialDeep`
Type-aware lint rules and the parser that lets ESLint read TypeScript
Community type declarations for JavaScript packages that ship none

explanation: These packages fill different gaps. zod checks untrusted data at runtime and derives types with `z.infer`. type-fest adds utility types the standard library lacks. typescript-eslint brings linting, including rules that need type information. `@types/*` packages from DefinitelyTyped describe JavaScript libraries without bundled types.
reference: zod, type-fest, typescript-eslint and DefinitelyTyped documentation

options.text: `as` only works on object types, not primitives
options.why: Assertions work on any type; the problem is how far apart the types are.

options.text: `string` and `number` don't overlap (TS2352); going via `unknown` bypasses that check
options.why: A single assertion must go to a type that overlaps; every type overlaps `unknown`.

options.text: Both convert the string to the number 42 at runtime
options.why: Assertions are erased; no conversion happens, so `b` is still the string `"42"`.

options.text: The second line fails too, because double assertions through `unknown` are disallowed whenever `strict` is enabled
options.why: Double assertions compile in every mode, which is why they deserve scrutiny.

explanation: A type assertion is allowed only when one type is assignable to the other. `string` and `number` don't overlap, so tsc reports TS2352 ("Conversion of type 'string' to type 'number' may be a mistake…"). Asserting to `unknown` first satisfies both steps, because everything is assignable to `unknown`. Nothing changes at runtime: `b` is still `"42"`. A double assertion is a deliberate escape hatch that silences a real warning.

stem: Writing `const user = body as unknown as User;` makes TypeScript insert a runtime check that `body` really has the shape of `User`.

options.text: True
options.why: Assertions, including double ones, are erased at compile time; nothing is checked.

options.text: False
options.why: The assertion only changes the static type; validate with a schema or type guard to check at runtime.

explanation: Type assertions are compile-time only and emit no code. `as unknown as User` tells the compiler to trust you, so if `body` is malformed the error appears later, far from its cause. Validate untrusted data at the boundary (a schema library such as zod, or a hand-written type guard) and let the validated type flow from there.
